turns.text: What do you remember about the day you first arrived in Beidahuang? What did you see, smell, and feel as you stepped off the train?

The train doors opened and a sharp wind hit my face, colder than anything I’d known in Shanghai. The platform was just packed earth, not concrete, and my shoes slipped a little as I stepped down. I smelled coal smoke, wet mud, and something sour—maybe fermented grain from the nearby storage. My hands went numb almost immediately, and I remember how my city coat felt thin as paper against that wind. The sky looked huge, grey, and unforgiving, with nothing to break it except a few squat buildings and endless flat land stretching out. I saw other young people, some with faces pinched from the cold, some trying to look brave. I felt small, exposed, and suddenly very far from home. My stomach twisted with hunger and nerves, and I kept my eyes on my feet so I wouldn’t trip in front of the local cadres who had come to meet us.

I can almost feel the shock of that cold and the strangeness of the open land after a crowded city. You mentioned the sour smell—did that scent become part of your daily life there, or did it fade as you settled in?

The sour smell never really faded; if anything, it became sharper as the seasons changed. It seeped into our clothes and even our hair, especially on days when the wind carried it straight from the storage sheds. Some mornings, I woke up with the taste of it in my mouth, and it mixed with the scent of damp straw in the dormitory. After a while, I noticed it less, but sometimes—especially when I was tired or homesick—it would hit me all over again, and I’d remember how far I was from the sweet, oily smells of street food back home. The locals hardly seemed to notice it, but for me, it was a constant reminder that I didn’t belong.

Homesickness sounds like it clung to you, even in the air you breathed. You mentioned waking up in the dormitory—what was it like living there with other sent-down youth? Did you feel any sense of solidarity, or was it mostly tension and competition?

At first, the dormitory felt as cold inside as it was outside. We slept on rough wooden planks with thin quilts, packed close together so our elbows touched. At night, I could hear people crying quietly, trying to muffle the sound. There was some comfort in knowing I wasn’t the only one who missed home, but there was also tension—everyone was scared of making mistakes, of being singled out by the local cadres, or of not working hard enough. Sometimes we whispered about Shanghai, about food or family, and for a few minutes it felt like we were back in the city together. But there were arguments, too, over chores or over who got the least moldy steamed bun. In the mornings, when we lined up for roll call, I could see in their faces that most of us were just trying to survive the day.

The way you describe the quiet crying and the arguments over something as small as a steamed bun makes the struggle so real. You mentioned being afraid of being singled out by the local cadres—can you remember a specific time when you or someone else was called out, and how that changed the mood in the dorm afterward?

One morning, just before dawn, the door banged open and the local cadre marched in, boots heavy on the boards. He held up a ragged shirt and said someone had stolen it from the drying line. His voice was loud enough to rattle the windows, and he demanded the thief step forward. No one moved. I could feel the girl next to me shaking, though I didn’t know if it was fear or cold.

He started pointing at us, one by one, barking questions—where were you last night, what did you see, do you know who did it? When no one confessed, he said we’d all lose our breakfast ration until the shirt was returned. That day, the silence in the dorm was thick as porridge. People avoided each other’s eyes. Some whispered that it was a setup, that the shirt never existed, just an excuse to remind us who was in charge. No one dared talk about home that night. Even the crying stopped, replaced by a heavy, watchful quiet. I remember lying awake, staring at the ceiling, feeling that the walls had ears.

That sense of suspicion and fear must have changed how you trusted the people around you. After that incident, did you notice people behaving differently—maybe keeping more to themselves, or watching what they said?

After that, everything felt different. People spoke in shorter sentences, if at all, and even when we were alone, our voices dropped to whispers. I saw some of the boys start to hide their food or small belongings under their bedding, even if no one had ever touched their things before. At night, instead of sharing stories about home, most people just turned to the wall and tried to sleep. It was like we all built invisible fences around ourselves. Sometimes, someone would glance at the door before saying anything at all, as if the cadre might burst in again at any moment. I felt lonelier than ever, because even though we were packed together, it was as if we each had our own little island of fear.

It’s strange how quickly fear can build walls where there used to be none. I remember feeling the same thing when a new instructor arrived—suddenly, every conversation felt risky, even a joke or a complaint. I started to watch my own words so closely that sometimes I’d forget what I’d meant to say in the first place. When you’re always glancing at the door or checking who’s listening, it’s easy to lose any sense of real connection. Even the smallest comfort, like laughing about something silly, could feel dangerous. It made me wonder if that kind of suspicion was what the Party wanted from us all along—everyone isolated, too wary to join together.

Your words make me think about how much trust shapes daily life, and how its loss leaves people isolated even in a crowd. You mentioned catching yourself before saying things, even forgetting what you meant to say—was there ever a moment when you almost slipped and said something risky, and how did you handle that?

There was one afternoon in the fields, when we were bent over pulling weeds and the sun was beating down. Someone muttered a joke about how in Shanghai, at least, you could find shade under the eaves of tall buildings. Without thinking, I almost added, “And you didn’t have to worry about someone spying on you for every little thing.” The words were right on my tongue, but I caught myself just in time. My heart thudded so hard I thought everyone could hear it. I pretended to cough, then bent lower over the weeds, my face burning. For the rest of the day, I barely spoke. That night, I replayed it over and over, wondering what would have happened if I’d actually said it out loud—whether someone would have reported me, or if I’d lose my work points, or worse. After that, I learned to rehearse even the simplest things in my head before I spoke, just in case.

That feeling—your heart pounding so hard you think it must be visible—was something I lived with too. It’s not just fear of being punished; it’s the fear that even a stray word could change your fate. I remember once someone let slip that they missed reading novels from before the Cultural Revolution, and the silence that followed was like a slap. No one reported her, but after that, people kept their distance, as if her longing for old stories might be contagious. I started to believe that even my thoughts could betray me if I wasn’t careful. When you live like that, always rehearsing, do you think you can ever really go back to trusting your own voice?

I wonder about that all the time—how much a person’s inner life can change under pressure, and whether it’s possible to unlearn that self-censorship. When you finally left Beidahuang, did you find it difficult to speak freely again, or did the habit of caution stay with you for years afterward?
